title: Beyond Persuasion: Evidence Type Affects Impressions of a Message Source
author: Jenna Clark
license_note: Confirmed via CrossRef DOI metadata: dx.doi.org/10.17504/protocols.io.7rahm2e

steps.title: Prepare Qualtrics survey
steps.instruction: Create a Qualtrics questionnaire that includes (a) a vignette where a target solicits advice and a source provides either a narrative or statistical argument, optionally preceded by a one‑line frame clarifying the desired advice type; (b) competence and warmth rating items for the source; (c) additional individual‑difference scales; (d) for the financial‑decision study, three argument topics (financial decisions, education, weight loss) each presented in narrative and statistical form, with 1‑to‑7 rating scales for multiple dimensions and for perceived basis (research/statistics vs personal experience/stories); and (e) a final demographics section.

steps.title: Recruit participants
steps.instruction: Invite participants to access the survey online via Qualtrics for the online studies; for Study 3b, bring participants into a laboratory, informing them that some will act as writers (who will compose a passage on active learning and be available at a pre‑chosen time) and others as readers.

steps.title: Present vignette and argument
steps.instruction: Online: ask participants to imagine performing a task online with an unknown interaction partner, then display the vignette and the assigned narrative or statistical argument on active learning (or the appropriate topic). Lab (Study 3b): have all participants view the “reader” instructions, randomly assign each to a competitive or cooperative task, then show both narrative and statistical arguments labeled as outputs of two potential partners.

steps.title: Collect argument ratings
steps.instruction: Ask participants to rate the argument on all required dimensions using the specified scales (e.g., 1 = not at all to 7 = very much for competence, warmth, quality, etc.). For the financial/education/weight‑loss arguments, also have them rate the extent the argument seems based on research/statistics versus personal experience/stories on a 1‑to‑7 scale.

steps.title: Obtain task and partner choices
steps.instruction: For the active‑learning study, have participants choose between two possible tasks to complete with their partner and rate those tasks on the same dimensions. In Study 3b, after viewing both arguments, require participants to select which partner they wish to work with on the assigned task.

steps.title: Administer final questionnaires
steps.instruction: Present the competence and warmth measures for the source (if not already collected), followed by any remaining individual‑difference questionnaires and the demographic questionnaire.
